messages.text: Will a power spike fry the whole miner?

Great question — this is actually one of the Rev 6.1's real design wins.

**There's an onboard F1 fuse** — a small automotive-style blade fuse sitting right on the board, next to the yellow XT30 power input. It's the first thing in the power path.

If a spike hits:
- **The F1 fuse blows** — sacrificing itself
- The A., ESP32, and everything behind it are protected
- You replace a cheap fuse, not a $249 miner

Cheaper home miners often skip this entirely — a spike goes straight into the electronics and **kills the whole board**.

The fuse is *on the miner board itself* (not in the PSU or on the cable) — so protection travels with the unit regardless of what power supply you use.
What stops it from overheating or dying?

Several layers work together — here's the stack:

**1. Spring-mounted heatsink**
Springs press the sink evenly across all four BM1370 dies — no one "hot corner" chip cooking faster than the rest. Result: ~57 °C at full 6 TH/s.

**2. Custom BSB airflow shroud**
A co-designed duct routes cold fan air *directly onto the voltage regulators* — the part that quietly kills most small miners first. No dedicated VRM cooling = first thing to fry. Here it gets its own airflow.

**3. VRM temps held in check**
~54 °C on the voltage regulators at full load — the usual first-to-fail part is the one they actually cooled.

**4. Upgraded power path (Rev 6.1 fix)**
The old Rev 5 used an 8 A barrel jack that sagged and melted under load. Rev 6.1 swaps in:
- **XT30 connector rated 15 A**
- **Thicker PCB (1 oz copper / 2 mm FR-4)** for cleaner power delivery

Input holds a steady **11.9 V** at full load — no brown-outs, no cooked connector.

**5. Oversized MEANWELL PSU**
350 W supply feeding a ~100 W miner — loafing at ~30% load, running cool and long-lived.

It's ~40–45 dB doing all of this — quiet enough for a desk.
Is the included power supply actually reliable?

Yes — and it's meaningfully overspec'd for this job.

**What's included:** MEANWELL LRS-350-12 — 350 W / 29 A, UL/CE/UKCA certified. Industrial-grade, open-frame supply.

**Why it matters:**
- The miner draws ~100 W at full load
- That's roughly **30% of the PSU's cap····** — it's barely working
- Supplies run coolest and longest when they're not being pushed hard

**The contrast with cheaper bundles:**
Competitors often ship 99–124 W bricks with a ~100 W miner. At that load, the brick is already at or past its safe sustained limit — running hot, stressed, and likely to fail 24/7. When the PSU goes, it can take the miner with it.

**Bonus — overclock headroom:**
The same LRS-350-12 fed a research run that pushed well past 6 TH/s. So if you ever want to experiment with overclocking via the open firmware, the PSU isn't your bottleneck.

**Bottom line:** It's a real industrial supply loafing at a third of its rating — not a wall-wart afterthought. It ships in the box, so you're genuinely ready to plug in and run day one.
Is it quiet enough to run in my office?

Yes — it's genuinely desk-friendly.

**The numbers:**
- ~40–45 dB at full load (6 TH/s)
- That's quiet-room level — comparable to a gentle fan or background hum

**Why it stays quiet:**
The spring-mounted heatsink + one large front fan setup moves enough air slowly — no tiny screaming fan trying to compensate for a undersized heatsink.

**The full picture:**
- **0.5 kg** — palm-sized, ~20 cm long
- Sits on its **3D-printed BSB stand**, screen angled toward you
- **1.9″ color LCD** shows live hashrate, temps, WiFi — glanceable from your desk, no laptop needed
- Connects via **WiFi 2.4 GHz** — no ethernet cable to route

One honest note: ~40–45 dB is *quiet*, not *silent*. In a dead-silent room you'll notice it. In a normal office with any background noise — keyboard, music, AC — it disappears.

Most owners run it on a desk or shelf without a second thought.
